sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye goes straight to the dark middle card, "Woodland loop". It is the odd one of three. The page reads as a list of walking routes to choose from. The middle card looks either featured or as if it came from another stylesheet, and nothing on the page says which. The overall feel is neat but uneven.

Job (assumed): a page or section that lets a visitor compare three walking routes and open one.

The whole piece:
1. Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this piece is for? yes
2. Do the image and headline make one idea? yes (there is no main image)
3. Does every element do a job? yes. The cards are too tall for their content, but that belongs to arrangement.
4. Do type, colours and shapes share one mood and era? no. The middle card has a serif heading, a pill-shaped amber outline button and square corners, while the others have a bold sans heading, a filled blue rounded button and rounded corners.
5. Is the copy finished? yes
6. Does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears? no. The middle card's fill, corners, border, heading face and size, padding and button all differ.
7. Do the colours and shapes carry the mood? yes
8. Does each heading name its section? yes

Bash was refused, so I could not run the crop or entries scripts. The image is one screen (about 1280×800), so I judged from the whole image, and the deep read comes from my knowledge of the cited sources, not from opened entries.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element (primary buttons, links, cards, section headings, error states) look the same everywhere it appears?** No.
   - **Where:** the middle card (about x 460–820, y 160–598) breaks the pattern the two outer cards set in every respect:
     - it has a dark charcoal fill where the others are white;
     - its corners are square and its border is a lighter 1 px line, where the others have rounded corners and a grey border;
     - its heading is a serif at a larger size ("Woodland loop" at about y 198), where the others use a bold sans at about y 211;
     - its padding is much tighter: text starts about 15 px from the card edge, against about 34 px in the others;
     - its button is an amber pill in outline, where the other two are filled blue rounded rectangles.
   - **What the viewer meets:** the card looks featured or recommended, but no label says so or why. The viewer has to guess whether this route is special or the page is broken. The signals also contradict each other. The loudest card has the quietest button, because an outline button reads as secondary, while the two plain cards get the strong filled blue. "View route" also stops looking like one action repeated three times.
   - **Why:** Nielsen heuristic 4, consistency and standards. Repeated items should follow one programme (Müller-Brockmann, Gerstner).
   - **Fix:** if Woodland loop is not meant to stand out, rebuild it from the same card component as the others. If it is meant to stand out, keep the shared structure (corners, padding, heading face, filled primary button), signal the emphasis in one way only (a tint, border colour or "Recommended" tag), and say why it is singled out.
   - **Kind:** defect. **Weight:** major.
2. **Apart from the pictures, do the type, colors, and shapes share one mood and era, so the piece reads as one whole rather than a collage?** No.
   - **Where:** the middle card brings a second visual language into a page that is otherwise plain modern UI: a bookish serif display face, amber on charcoal, and a pill shape, set beside a grotesque sans, corporate blue and small-radius rectangles.
   - **What the viewer meets:** the three cards look like two different products placed side by side, not one set of options.
   - **Why:** art-direction principles of unity and thematic coherence. The catalog marks these as off-list sources, so this is my judgement as a designer.
   - **Fix:** pick one type family and one accent colour for the set. If the serif or amber is wanted for brand character, use it on all three cards, not on one.
   - **Kind:** taste. **Weight:** minor, because fixing finding 1 removes most of it.

**What's working.**
- The page heading "Walking routes" and the route descriptions are plain and concrete: distance, terrain and amenities ("two steep climbs and a cafe at the far end"). A first-time viewer can tell straight away what the page is for and compare the routes on terms they care about.
- The two outer cards are a clean, consistent component that the middle card can be rebuilt from.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (one mood and era; each kind of element looks the same everywhere), 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No. The "Woodland loop" heading (x ≈ 475–690, y ≈ 183–215) is in a serif that looks about 30 px. That is roughly the size of the page title "Walking routes" (x ≈ 64–297, y ≈ 78–112). It is also clearly bigger than its sibling headings "Cliff path" and "Canal towpath" (sans bold, about 24 px). So one heading level, the route name, is set two ways, and one of them matches the level above it.
   - **What the viewer meets:** the page title loses its place as the top level. "Woodland loop" reads as a second headline or a featured route, not one of three routes to compare, and nothing on the page says it is featured. Someone comparing three routes gets one that is louder than the others for no reason they can see. This adds to the dark card's value contrast and the yellow outline button, so the middle card takes the first look away from the page title.
   - **Why:** each level of importance should be clearly different from the next at a glance (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*; "Visual hierarchy has distinct levels"). Here two levels overlap, and one level is split across two treatments.
   - **Fix:** set all three route names in one style, at one size clearly below the page title. If Woodland loop really is the recommended route, say so in words (for example a "Recommended" label) and keep its heading at the card level. Then the emphasis carries a reason and doesn't break the type scale.
   - Defect. Weight: major. Three peer options that look unequal, with one heading competing with the page title, change how a walker reads and chooses.

**What's working.** The white cards have a clean three-step ladder: bold title, regular grey body text, and a solid blue button. Each step differs in size and in weight or colour, so in each card the reader goes name → description → action without hesitating. The page title also stands clearly above the white-card headings, by size and weight.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the dark middle card is meant to be a "featured" or selected state, or is just a styling mistake. Check the live page or the spec. If it's a selected or hover state, the heading-size collision is still there but would show up less often.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (text levels distinct, no near-equal sizes)

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do all blocks take their edges and gaps from one grid; is every element exactly aligned or clearly off; do lines in neighbouring columns share baselines?** (lines 1–3, one problem). The row itself is on a grid: three equal cards (about x 64–427, 459–821, 853–1216) with even 32 px gutters, and the page heading lines up with card 1 at x 64. The grid breaks inside the middle card. Its content starts about 16 px from its left edge (x 475), while the outer cards start about 34 px in (x 98, x 887). Its title sits about 14 px higher (cap top around y 185 against y 199), its body lines sit about 9 px higher (y 244 against 253), and its button top sits at about y 337 against 346. Those gaps are too small to read as a deliberate break, so the row's three titles, descriptions and buttons miss each other by a few pixels. The viewer sees one card that looks pasted in from another layout, and the eye stutters as it scans across the row. Sources: Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design* (one grid governs the page); Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I (a near-miss makes the eye waver); Gerstner, *Designing Programmes* (repeated elements follow one program). Fix: give all three cards the same inner padding and vertical rhythm so titles, first lines and buttons share one line across the row. If the middle card is meant to be featured, mark it with fill only and keep its geometry. **Defect. Major.**
2. **Do only related elements look alike, with no accidental groups?** (line 6). The three cards are the same kind of thing, three routes. The middle one changes everything at once: dark fill, square corners instead of rounded, a serif title instead of the sans, an outlined pill button in yellow instead of a filled blue rectangle, and different padding. With no label like "Featured" or "Recommended", it reads as a different kind of item, such as an ad or a promo, rather than one of three choices. The two outer cards also pair up as a set, with the middle one as the odd one out. Source: Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*. Fix: if one route should stand out, change one property (fill or a badge) and keep the shared card system. If none should, make all three match. Whether emphasis is wanted at all is a hierarchy question. **Defect. Major.**
3. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas?** (line 9). Each card is about 440 px tall (y 160–598), but its content ends at about y 394. That leaves roughly 200 px of empty, boxed-in space at the bottom of every card. Below the row there is about another 200 px of open page. The empty space ends up trapped inside the borders, where it does nothing. It makes the cards look unfinished, as if an image or details failed to load. Source: Ruder, *Typography: A Manual of Design*, "Contrasts" (white space gathered, not scattered). Fix: fit the card height to its content and let the leftover space sit open on the page, or fill the area with what a route card would normally carry (map, distance, difficulty). If something is meant to load there, this isn't the design's fault; see below. **Defect. Minor.**

**What's working.**
- The outer frame is on a grid: equal card widths, equal 32 px gutters, and the heading flush with the first card's left edge at x 64. The structure is sound once the middle card's insides follow it.
- The spacing inside the outer cards groups things correctly. The title sits nearer its description than the description sits to the button, and the heading-to-row gap (about 50 px) is clearly larger than any gap inside a card, so each card reads as one unit.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The empty lower half of every card may be space for a route map or image that didn't load in this capture. Check in a live browser. If nothing is meant to load there, finding 3 stands as written.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 9 yes, 4 no (one grid governs the page; aligned or clearly off; baselines across columns; only related elements look alike), 0 unsure. White space gathered is also reported above as finding 3, so the director should count it as a fifth no: 13 lines, 8 yes, 5 no.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the typefaces follow one plan, one family or a few plainly different faces, with no face that nearly matches another and no extra unrelated face?** No. "Woodland loop" (heading of the middle card, about x 475–690, y 185–215) is set in a serif display face. All the other text on the page is in one sans: the page title, the other two card headings, all body copy and the buttons. The serif is used once, on one card out of three. So it doesn't read as a deliberate contrast between levels, like serif headings over sans text. It looks like the middle card came from a different system or failed to inherit the page style. The viewer can't tell whether "Woodland loop" is special, featured or sponsored, or just broken. The serif heading also reads larger and lighter than its siblings, "Cliff path" and "Canal towpath", so three headings at the same level don't look like the same level. Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 7–8: faces should relate by concord or by clear contrast, and an extra unrelated face used once has no relationship to the rest. Fix: set "Woodland loop" in the same sans, size and weight as the other card headings. If the middle card really is featured, mark that with something the system already has, such as a label or the dark ground on its own, not with a new typeface. Convention. Weight: major.
2. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line?** No. All three blurbs end with one word alone on the last line:
   - "end." in Cliff path (about x 98, y 302)
   - "metres." in Woodland loop (about x 475, y 294)
   - "bicycles." in Canal towpath (about x 887, y 302)

   "end." is the worst: four letters under two full lines, which leaves a ragged hole above the button. Across a row of identical cards the repetition looks careless. Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, §2.4.2. Fix: pull a second word onto each last line. Use `text-wrap: pretty` or a non-breaking space before the last word, or edit the copy so the paragraphs end on a fuller line. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The body copy is one size, weight and grey in all three cards. It's set flush left at an easy line spacing and about 36–47 characters a line, which suits text in several columns (Bringhurst gives 40 to 50). The blurbs read in one pass, and the three can be compared line for line.
- The body grey on white and the light grey on charcoal both look well above 4.5:1, so the muted body colour sets the text back behind the headings without making it faint.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (typefaces follow one plan; paragraphs and columns break cleanly).

The color section finds one problem, a major one: the middle card's "View route" button doesn't match the other two.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does each color that is meant to match look the same wherever it sits? No.**
   - **Where:** The three "View route" buttons do the same job. Two are filled blue with white text (98–230 × 346–394 and 887–1019 × 346–394). The middle one is an amber outline with amber text (about 475–610 × 337–389). The pattern repeats in the cards themselves: the outer two have soft blue-gray borders and rounded corners, while the middle card has a flat gray edge and square corners.
   - **What the viewer gets:** The only strong colors on the page, blue and amber, are both spent on buttons for one action. That suggests the middle action is something different, which it isn't. The middle card also has the most visual weight on the page but the weakest button style (an outline). So it's unclear whether this is the recommended route or a leftover from another theme.
   - **Why:** The Simultaneous contrast entry (Albers, *Interaction of Color*) covers colors that look different because of what surrounds them. This one is a literal mismatch, not a perceived one, so the finding is common sense rather than a sourced rule. One action should have one color.
   - **Fix:** Use the same action color on all three buttons. If the middle route really is featured, keep that emphasis on the card (fill, plus a label saying why) and give its button the same filled style, adapted to work on the dark fill. Match the card edges too.
   - **Kind and weight:** Defect. Major.

**What's working.**
- **Value range:** It's strong and clean. The near-black slate card, white cards, dark gray titles and mid-gray body text would still read clearly in grayscale.
- **The dark card's fill:** It's a dark slate gray, not pure black. That keeps the jump against the white page from glaring and lets the light-gray body text on it stay soft but legible.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (each color meant to match looks the same wherever it sits).

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photos, illustrations, icons, logos or marks. It shows a heading and three route cards with only text and buttons.

**Findings**
None.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Each card has a large empty area below its button (about y 400–598 in all three). If these cards are meant to hold a route photo or map, the picture may not have loaded when the screenshot was taken. Check the page in a live browser to see whether an image belongs there. If none does, the empty space is a layout question for `arrangement`, not for this section.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has three "View route" buttons, one per route card.

**Findings**
1. **Is exactly one button styled as the primary action, with every other action styled lower?** No. "View route" is the same action on all three cards, but it is styled two ways.
   - **Where:** on "Cliff path" (about 98,346, 132×48 px) and "Canal towpath" (about 887,346) it is a filled blue button with small rounded corners. On "Woodland loop" (about 475,337, 136×52 px) it is a yellow outlined pill on the dark card.
   - **What the viewer meets:** an outline is the lower-emphasis style (Material Design 3, "Buttons": filled for the most important action, outlined or text for lesser ones). So the screen says opening Woodland loop matters less than opening the other two. Yet the dark card is the first thing the eye lands on. The viewer gets two signals that disagree: this route is featured, but its action is secondary. Or they wonder whether the yellow pill does something different from the blue buttons. The same component in two looks also breaks the pattern that lets someone scan a card grid and know what each button does.
   - **Note on the rule:** a filled button repeated once per card in a list of equal items is the normal pattern, so the two blue buttons are not the fault. The fault is the mismatch.
   - **Fix:** give every card's "View route" the same treatment. If Woodland loop really is the featured route, show that through the card itself, such as a label or its position, not by demoting its button.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect (mixed signal about rank and sameness), resting on convention (Material Design 3 emphasis levels). Minor: the buttons still read as pressable and clearly labelled, so walkers can still open every route.

**What's working.**
- Every "View route" button looks pressable. Each is a solid or clearly outlined shape with bold text, about 130×48 px, well above the 24 px minimum (WCAG 2.5.8), and set apart from the description above it.
- The button text is short and repeated, but each button sits inside a card under the route name, so its purpose is clear from context (WCAG 2.4.4, link purpose in context). Nothing has to be remembered from another screen.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicators on the three buttons. They are the only interactive elements, so keyboard users depend on them. Check that each shows an outline at least 2 px thick at 3:1 contrast, including the yellow pill on the dark card.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 1 no (one primary action, others styled lower), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
